**Refined prompt:** Confirm from the code whether a non-author can edit an article through this API, with the exact lines that prove it; then say who the possible actors are and whether the system can tell you who did it. Incident triage, not a patch.

Yes. It's not a bug you got unlucky with — `PUT /api/articles/:slug` has no ownership check at all. Any valid token can edit any article.

**The three lines that prove it**

1. `src/article/article.module.ts:27` — the route *is* in `AuthMiddleware`'s list, so the caller had to present a working token.
2. `src/article/article.controller.ts:59-63` — the handler signature is `update(@Param() params, @Body('article') articleData)`. There is no `@User('id')`. The handler never learns who is calling, so it cannot compare.
3. `src/article/article.service.ts:190-195` — `findOne({slug})` → `Object.assign(toUpdate, articleData)` → `save()`. Nothing touches `article.author`.

The `@ApiResponse({ status: 403, description: 'Forbidden.' })` on `article.controller.ts:58` documents a check that was never written. This is the exact incident already recorded in `LESSONS.md:18-27`.

**Who could have done it**

- Any registered user, on any account. That's the floor.
- Possibly wider: `src/config.ts` isn't in this workspace, only `src/config.ts.example:1` — `export const SECRET = 'secret-key'`. If the deployed instance still uses that value, anyone can forge a token for any user id and never needed an account. Worth checking your actual deploy first; it changes the suspect set from "our users" to "anyone".
- `.claude/knowledge/auth.md:10-12` puts token expiry at 60 days, so a token leaked two months ago still works. I did not open `user.service.ts` this pass to verify that number.

**They could have changed more than the text.** Because of the `Object.assign` at `article.service.ts:192` and no validation pipe, any column on `ArticleEntity` in the request body is persisted — including `favoriteCount` (`article.entity.ts:45`) and the `author` FK (`article.entity.ts:37-38`). If the article's author still reads as you, that only means they didn't bother. Same root cause as `LESSONS.md:39-47`.

**Can you find out who? Not from this app.**

There is no request logging, no audit table — grep for `logger|Logger|morgan|audit` across `src/` returns nothing, and `src/main.ts` wires up only CORS, the `/api` prefix, and Swagger. The single trace is `article.updated`, stamped by `@BeforeUpdate()` at `article.entity.ts:29-32`. That gives you a timestamp and nothing else. Query `updated` on the affected row, then take that timestamp to your reverse proxy or host access logs — that's the only place a source IP could exist.

**Related exposure, same root cause,** since you'll want the blast radius: `DELETE /articles/:slug` is identical (`article.module.ts:26`, `controller.ts:68-71`, `service.ts:197-199`). `.claude/knowledge/auth.md:47-49` also claims `DELETE /users/:slug` is entirely unguarded and deletes by email — I did not read the user module this pass to confirm that one.

The fix is already queued as an active item in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md:10-12`, marked design-first. One wrinkle worth knowing before that design: `author` is a plain `@ManyToOne` with no `eager: true` (`article.entity.ts:37`), so today's `findOne({slug})` returns it as `undefined` — the check needs `relations: ['author']` or it will throw rather than deny (`LESSONS.md:68-76`).

Want me to draft that ownership check for `PUT`/`DELETE /articles/:slug`? I'd write it as a proposal against `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` rather than editing the services directly, since that item says design first.
